analysis.one_liner: Requires captions, audio description, and accessible design across online video, TVs, and video conferencing for deaf and blind viewers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in November 2022 with seven Democratic senators behind it, was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would update a 2010 disability-access law to cover the internet era. It would require closed captioning on online video, audio description (a narrated track describing what's on screen) on both TV and streaming, dedicated caption and audio-description buttons on remotes and devices, built-in captioning in video conferencing services, American Sign Language access to 911, and a larger program distributing equipment to people who are DeafBlind. It also lets video conferencing providers be charged into the fund that pays for telecommunications relay services, and gives the FCC stronger enforcement tools. It was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: People who are deaf, hard of hearing, blind, low-vision, or DeafBlind gain far fuller access to streaming video, television, video calls, and emergency services. Caption quality rules would extend to all online programming, audio description would become standard on TV and the internet, devices would need dedicated accessible controls, and ASL users would get direct video access to 911. Older Americans and accessibility advocates are named stakeholders in the bill's advisory committees.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the FCC to mandate closed captioning on video programming delivered over the internet, with quality rules extended to all online programming and a schedule of deadlines phasing in over several years [S3].
Requires audio description for both televised and internet-delivered video programming, so blind and low-vision viewers hear narration of key visual elements [S2] [S3].
Requires TVs, streaming devices, and remotes to carry dedicated, tactilely identifiable buttons for captions and audio description, with settings that persist across apps and restarts [S3].
Extends accessibility obligations to video conferencing services, requiring built-in captioning and compatibility with screen readers, braille displays, and third-party interpreting services [S3].

Directs the FCC to ensure full, equal, and direct access to 911 for ASL users, including location transmission at the same speed as a voice call, and doubles funding for the National DeafBlind Equipment Distribution Program from $10 million to $20 million [S3].
Requires video conferencing providers to contribute to the Telecommunications Relay Services fund and strengthens FCC enforcement and penalty authority over accessibility violations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Streaming and online video platforms would bear captioning and audio description production costs, including for popular user-generated channels above a $1 million revenue threshold. TV manufacturers and consumer electronics makers would redesign remotes and devices. Video conferencing providers would build in captioning and pay into the relay services fund. The law includes economic-burden exemption petitions and long phase-in deadlines, and the FCC advisory committees would include industry representatives.
analysis.who_pays_short: Streaming platforms, device makers, conferencing providers

drawbacks.text: Captioning and audio description every online program — including live and near-live content and large user-generated channels — is expensive, and production quality for live events is technically hard; the bill responds with a user-generated-video revenue threshold and FCC economic-burden exemptions [S3].

Requiring dedicated physical buttons on every remote and device manufactured or imported into the U.S. imposes design and manufacturing costs across the consumer electronics industry, including on devices sold to people who never use the features [S3].
The bill uses lengthy timelines — advisory committees, reports, then FCC rulemaking with final deadlines up to six years out — so many accessibility gains would not arrive quickly [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For tens of millions of Americans with sensory disabilities, the bill addresses a real gap: the 2010 accessibility law largely predates the streaming era, and the CRS summary states it expands requirements for online captioning and audio description [S2]. The costs fall on large, well-resourced industries in the form of production and engineering expenses, softened by exemptions, phase-ins, and industry seats on the FCC advisory committees [S3]. The most legitimate complaint is the slow timetable rather than the goal itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey introduced the bill on November 17, 2022, the final weeks of the 117th Congress, with six cosponsors: five Senate Democrats and one Independent [S1] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].
The CRS summary describes the bill as expanding and establishing new accessibility requirements for communications technologies, including online closed captioning and audio description [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Streaming and online video platforms, consumer electronics manufacturers, and video conferencing providers are better off, because they avoided new captioning, audio description, device-design, and relay-fund obligations. Viewers with disabilities gained nothing from the bill's failure.

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to update the 2010 communications accessibility law.

for.name: Sens. Whitehouse, Warren, Sanders, Wyden, Duckworth, and Feinstein
for.role: Cosponsors (5 of 48 Senate Democrats; 1 of 2 Senate Independents)

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action on it — no hearing, no markup — leaving it to die when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors were Democrats or Independents; no Republican cosponsored, and no votes ever occurred to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill would require closed captioning and audio description on internet-delivered video, including large user-generated channels above $1 million in revenue, with quality rules and enforcement. These compliance costs are the price of deaf and blind viewers getting equal access to online programming.

They would have to build in captioning, support assistive technologies, and for the first time pay into the Telecommunications Relay Services fund. The obligation transfers part of the cost of deaf-access services onto the industry.

Every covered device and remote sold or imported in the U.S. would need dedicated caption and audio description buttons, persistent settings, and compatibility with braille displays and hearing aids, raising design and manufacturing costs.

industries.industry: Captioning, audio description, and interpreting service agencies
industries.note: Expanded mandates across online video, TV, and video conferencing create a much larger market for these accessibility services, which the bill names as stakeholders on its advisory committees.
The bill expands relay services to cover communication facilitators for DeafBlind users, direct video calling, and ASL access to 911, funded through the relay services fund.
